title: 11 — Thermodynamic Witnesses of Entanglement
paragraphs: A New Way to Probe the Quantum World
Mia Stamatova

“Thermodynamics is a funny subject. The first time you go through it, you don’t understand it at all. The second time you go through it, you think you understand it, except for one or two small points. The third time you go through it, you know you don’t understand it, but by that time you are so used to it, it doesn’t bother you anymore.”
— _Arnold Sommerfeld_
The Beginning

Sommerfeld, one of the great thermodynamicists and quantum physicists of the twentieth century, managed to capture the spirit of thermodynamics in a single, wonderfully disarming observation. Thermodynamics really is peculiar. You quickly discover that the equations themselves are not the main obstacle; they are often quite manageable. The hard part is convincing yourself that the Universe must obey them whether it likes to or not!

Classical thermodynamics emerged in the nineteenth century from very practical concerns: heat engines, work, efficiency, and the nature of temperature. Its founders (Carnot, Joule, Kelvin, Clausius, etc.) were largely engineers and experimentalists, trying to make sense of what steam engines could and could not do. Their goal was not to uncover deep microscopic laws of physics, but to distill reliable, macroscopic rules from stubborn experimental facts. Remarkably, the rules they uncovered turned out to be far more general than anyone had reason to expect. Those macroscopic laws now govern systems far removed from the machinery that originally motivated their discovery: they apply to magnets, black holes, quantum gases, and the early Universe.

Even more strikingly, thermodynamics has become a kind of consistency test for theoretical physics. Any theory that claims to be fundamental must reproduce thermodynamic behaviour in the appropriate limit. For example, statistical mechanics earned its credibility by showing how the zeroth, first, and second laws emerge from large collections of microscopic degrees of freedom. Quantum mechanics is similarly constrained: it must recover classical equations of state at high temperatures, obey the third law as temperature approaches zero, and yield the correct expressions for heat capacities, pressures, and susceptibilities. Even general relativity and quantum field theory are judged in part by their ability to recover established thermodynamic relations in their semiclassical or macroscopic regimes, including black hole entropy, horizon thermodynamics, and the Clausius relation. There are numerous examples to illustrate this point, and it seems that, at least in light of our current understanding, any _new_ physics will obey the principles of thermodynamics.

It is worth pausing to appreciate just how bold this idea really is. To say that thermodynamics will survive future revolutions in physics is a bit like claiming that our current modes of transport will dominate indefinitely. History rarely rewards that kind of confidence. And yet physicists remain unusually sure that thermodynamics will endure. This quiet refusal to be overthrown is rather amazing, and it is part of what makes thermodynamics so unusual.
When Obeying the Rules Becomes Informative

This naturally raises a deeper question: can thermodynamics do _more_ than merely constrain new theories? Can it actively _lead_ us to new physics? The short answer is yes—and it already has. Although thermodynamics began as an experimental science, it entered a genuinely theoretical era in the mid-nineteenth century with the work of Maxwell, Boltzmann, and Gibbs. Their original aim was to interpret and justify the so-called phenomenological[1] formulation of thermodynamics, and in turn created an entirely new way of thinking about the subject. They used a bottom-up approach via arguments relying on microscopic, probability-based physics, which gave rise to what we now call statistical mechanics.

Quantum mechanics has also enriched the field of thermodynamics in a very concrete way, perhaps most strikingly through the prediction of Bose–Einstein condensation. In classical thermodynamics, lowering the temperature of a gas simply slows its atoms down; nothing fundamentally new is supposed to happen. But quantum mechanics tells a more surprising story. Particles like helium atoms or rubidium atoms, when cooled to billionths of a degree above absolute zero, cease to behave as distinguishable particles. Instead of behaving like many separate particles, they “agree” to occupy the exact same quantum state, forming a single, coherent entity spread out across the entire container. This is the Bose–Einstein condensate. Perhaps more remarkable than this phenomenon itself is how it was discovered. Bose–Einstein condensation was not stumbled upon experimentally and explained after the fact. Rather, it was predicted by following thermodynamic reasoning into the quantum domain, using the newly developed Bose–Einstein statistics. The theory said that below a certain critical temperature, the usual formulas for pressure and entropy simply couldn’t hold anymore; an entirely new phase of matter had to emerge. When scientists finally produced the first condensates in the 1990s, they found precisely the exotic behaviour that the thermodynamics calculation had demanded. This remains one of the cleanest examples of thermodynamic reasoning pointing the way to genuinely new physics.
Heat Capacity Knows More Than It Should

The success of Bose–Einstein condensation shows that quantum mechanics can enrich thermodynamics in powerful ways—but how about vice-versa? A group of physicists (Marcin Wiesniak, Vlatko Vedral, and Časlav Brukner) asked exactly this type of question in the early 2000s. Could thermodynamic quantities unto themselves reveal something fundamentally quantum? Their answer was unexpected and elegant. They demonstrated that thermodynamical quantities, such as heat capacity and internal energy, could be used as “witnesses” of quantum entanglement.

To see why this is surprising, we need to explain quantum entanglement a bit more. This phenomenon is the result of preparing two quantum systems in a joint state that cannot be factored into independent states for each system. Put simply, after certain interactions, the state of the full system contains correlations that don’t belong to either particle alone. The mathematics forces you to treat the pair (or many-body system) as a single entity, even if the components later become spatially separated. It is _the_ hallmark feature of quantum mechanics, and no classical theory is capable of reproducing the full strength of these correlations without abandoning assumptions about Nature, like the principle of locality or the idea that physical properties exist prior to measurement. Entanglement is therefore not merely a mathematical curiosity, but the defining feature of quantum mechanics—and a key resource in quantum technologies such as teleportation, error correction, and quantum computation.

Detecting entanglement, however, is notoriously difficult, especially in large systems. Typically, experimentalists have three options: Bell tests, full state quantum tomography, or witness-based tests. Naturally, each method has pros and cons. Bell tests are considered the classic, gold-standard method of detecting genuine entanglement. An entangled pair is sent to two distant labs, where experimentalists randomly and independently choose which property to measure (for example, different polarization angles for photons). If the particles only had classical instruction sets, there’s a strict mathematical limit, a Bell inequality, that caps how strong their correlations can be. Quantum mechanics predicts stronger correlations up to a value that breaks the classical bound. And when you actually perform the experiment, carefully ensuring the two labs can’t communicate and detecting essentially all particles, the data violates the Bell inequality. Although this is a very robust test of entanglement, it is difficult to scale experimentally due to noise and limited detection efficiency. Current technologies have a limit of around twenty qubits before it becomes infeasible to reliably violate Bell inequalities.

Full state quantum tomography faces similar challenges to Bell tests. It allows for a full reconstruction of the density matrix of the system (that is, a complete mathematical description) by measuring many copies of the state in different bases. One can then easily determine whether the system was entangled by mathematical inspection. This method is used widely for systems containing at most a handful of qubits, but it is impractical for large systems because the number of measurements required grows exponentially with system size.

Witness-based tests work by measuring a single quantity that must satisfy a strict bound if the system is unentangled, but is violated by certain entangled states. If an experiment gives a value on the _wrong_ side of that boundary, then the state is necessarily entangled. The basic idea is that unentangled states occupy a well-defined region in the space of all possible states. A witness is a _yes/no_ test that tells you whether your state lies outside that region. It’s much easier than reconstructing the full quantum state, but each witness only catches specific types of entanglement. One therefore designs a witness for the kind of state the experiment is meant to produce. It is somewhat like choosing a detector tuned to a particular signal, rather than hoping a single instrument will register everything.

A particularly interesting witness of entanglement is heat capacity, which is a measure of how much energy needs to be put into a system to raise its temperature by one degree. At very low temperatures, the behaviour of a system’s heat capacity is strongly constrained by the third law of thermodynamics. This law states that as temperature approaches absolute zero, a system’s entropy must also approach a constant value, which leads to the expectation that heat capacity must tend toward zero. This vanishing heat capacity reflects the fact that, near zero temperature, only a tiny number of low-energy excitations are available. Intuitively, you can understand this by imagining a box filled with loose puzzle pieces that is being shaken. The shaking represents thermal energy. When the box is shaken vigorously (i.e., at high temperature), the pieces constantly scramble into many different arrangements; they have enough energy to hop over little ridges and slide past one another, so the system explores a large number of configurations. As the shaking is reduced (i.e., as the temperature is lowered), the pieces still shift, but only among a smaller set of possibilities, because they no longer have the energy to move into configurations that require climbing over even small obstacles. If the temperature continues to be lowered, the shaking becomes too weak to lift the pieces out of their lowest resting spots, and the number of accessible arrangements dwindles rapidly. In the limit where the box is not shaken at all—this is analogous to absolute zero—the pieces are effectively locked into a single configuration that requires no extra energy to maintain. This captures the technical meaning of the third law of thermodynamics: as temperature approaches zero, the system’s accessible microstates collapse to just its lowest-energy configuration, and its capacity to absorb energy by rearranging itself (its heat capacity) necessarily vanishes.

Now here’s the ingenious insight. Let us assume that our system is in a separable state (in other words, not entangled). Then, as we discussed previously, the heat capacity should vanish as the temperature drops to zero. If this expectation fails, the logic backfires on our original assumption. We assumed the system was unentangled, worked out what thermodynamics then allows, and the experiment simply does not comply with that prediction. The only conclusion is that the assumption itself was wrong. This does not mean that heat capacity measures entanglement directly, but that no unentangled description can account for the observed thermodynamic response. When this happens, the measured heat capacity itself acts as an entanglement witness. Entanglement has left unavoidable thermodynamic fingerprints. The real punchline here is that these so-called fingerprints can be probed experimentally using very simple techniques, _without_ suffering the same ordeal as Bell tests and full state quantum tomography. What’s even more striking is that this approach is applicable at macroscopic scales—not just the micro, as is so often thought when discussing quantum phenomena.
Not Only Space, But Also Time?

One can push this same line of reasoning further by asking a slightly more subtle question: what if the correlations we are trying to detect are not only _spatial_, but also _temporal_? In other words, can thermodynamics tell us something about genuinely quantum correlations that link a system to its own past and future, rather than just to another particle sitting somewhere else in space? Remarkably, the answer is again _yes_—and the key player this time is the _complex_ heat capacity.

To appreciate why complex heat capacity is such a powerful idea, it helps to think carefully about what we normally mean by heat capacity in the first place. In everyday thermodynamics, heat capacity is an equilibrium notion. You nudge the temperature of a system slightly, wait patiently, and then measure how much its internal energy has changed once everything has settled down. Implicitly, you are giving the system as much time as it wants to relax. Any internal rearrangements, energy exchanges, or microscopic shuffling are assumed to have already happened by the time you look.

Real physical systems, however, rarely enjoy this luxury. Many systems relax slowly, possess internal bottlenecks, or contain degrees of freedom that respond on very different timescales. If you heat such a system in a time-dependent way—by gently oscillating the temperature, rather than changing it once and waiting—you can probe not just _how much_ energy the system can store, but _how_ and _how fast_ it reorganises that energy internally. The heat capacity stops being a static number and instead becomes a dynamical response, describing not just how much energy the system can absorb, but how quickly and reversibly it can do so.

This is where the idea of complex heat capacity enters the picture. The word “complex” here does not mean complicated; it means that the system’s response to a temperature change naturally splits into two qualitatively different parts. One part describes energy that is temporarily stored and then returned, much like a compressed spring that releases its energy when you let go. The other part describes energy that is irreversibly lost during the cycle, i.e., converted into microscopic disorder and never fully recovered. A helpful analogy is driving a car over a bumpy road. When the wheels hit a bump, part of the car’s kinetic energy goes into compressing the suspension. That energy is temporarily stored in the springs and then returned to the car’s motion as the suspension rebounds, lifting the car back up after the bump. This is a reversible process: energy flows into the suspension and then back out again without being permanently lost. At the same time, another part of the energy is dissipated by shock absorbers and friction, where it is converted into heat and cannot be recovered as mechanical motion. The ride you feel is the result of both processes acting together. Complex heat capacity captures this same split in thermodynamic form. Its real part corresponds to the energy that is temporarily stored and returned in step with the temperature modulation, while its imaginary part quantifies the energy that is irreversibly dissipated during each cycle.

Now, in classical thermodynamics or in quantum systems without entanglement, there are strong restrictions on how these two components can behave. The reason is essentially causal and statistical. If a system’s present response depends only on its current state and some classical memory of the past, then there is a limit to how strongly different moments in time can be correlated. The system may “remember” that it was heated recently, but that memory fades in a simple, well-behaved way. Technically, this shows up as constraints on how large the dissipative part of the response can be and how sharply it can vary with frequency of the applied temperature modulation.

Quantum mechanics allows for something more exotic. A system can become entangled with _itself_ across time, meaning that its state at one moment cannot be fully described without reference to its state at earlier or later moments. This is not merely a matter of delayed relaxation or sluggish dynamics. Instead, it reflects the fact that quantum evolution can generate correlations that have no classical analogue, even when looking at a single system rather than multiple particles. In this sense, different “time slices” of the system play the role that different spatial subsystems do in ordinary entanglement.

Temporal entanglement captures exactly this idea. Just as two spatially separated particles can share correlations that cannot be explained by local hidden variables,[2] a system evolving in time can display correlations between past and future observables that cannot be explained by any classical stochastic process. Importantly, these correlations are constrained by precise mathematical bounds if the system is assumed to be classical or separable in time. Violating those bounds means that no classical narrative can account for what is observed.

Complex heat capacity turns out to be very sensitive to these violations. When temperature is modulated, the way energy flows into and out of the system encodes information about correlations between energy fluctuations at different times. If those fluctuations are only classically correlated, the dissipative response stays within a well-defined range. But if the system exhibits genuine quantum correlations across time, the response can exceed those classical limits. In that case, the measured heat capacity behaves in a way that would be impossible if the system’s dynamics were merely classical, no matter how complicated or noisy. Just as before, the logic is clean and unforgiving: assume no temporal entanglement, derive a bound, and let the experiment decide whether that assumption survives contact with reality.

What makes this especially compelling is that the witness is again extremely economical. One does not need to reconstruct multi-time quantum states or perform elaborate sequences of measurements at carefully chosen moments. Instead, one probes the system with a gentle, macroscopic knob—an oscillating temperature—and observes how energy flows in response. The witness works not because thermodynamics has become “quantum-like” but because quantum mechanics has failed to hide itself from thermodynamics.

This closes a beautiful conceptual loop. Thermodynamics, born as a theory of steam engines and heat baths, turns out not only to survive quantum mechanics but to interrogate it. Equilibrium heat capacity exposes spatial entanglement hidden inside many-body ground states; complex heat capacity reveals entanglement embedded in dynamics and memory. The lesson is hard to miss: quantum correlations do not stay confined to qubits in clean, well-isolated laboratory settings. They leave measurable imprints in heat, work, and dissipation, exposing the limits of classical thermodynamics itself.
New Physics, Same Old Measures
All of this naturally raises a pragmatic question: if thermodynamics can witness spatial and temporal entanglement so efficiently, what can we actually _do_ with this knowledge?

The most immediate application lies in probing quantum correlations in systems that are otherwise experimentally inaccessible. Many physically relevant materials (e.g., strongly correlated solids, magnetic lattices, superconductors, and cold atomic ensembles) contain vast numbers of interacting degrees of freedom. In such systems, entanglement is believed to play a central role in phenomena like quantum phase transitions, topological order, and exotic lowtemperature phases. Yet direct entanglement detection is almost hopeless: Bell tests are infeasible, and quantum state tomography is out of the question. Heat capacity measurements, by contrast, are routine. Calorimetry is one of the most mature experimental techniques in physics. The fact that equilibrium heat capacity can act as an entanglement witness, therefore, opens a practical route to _experimentally certifying entanglement in bulk matter_, using tools that are bread-and-butter techniques for condensed-matter physicists.

This perspective reframes thermodynamic experiments that have been performed for decades. Anomalous low-temperature heat capacity curves, traditionally interpreted in terms of phonons, spin waves, or disorder, can now be re-examined through a quantuminformational lens. In certain regimes, what looks like an innocuous deviation from a simple power law may in fact signal entanglement woven into the ground state of the material. In this way, thermodynamics does not merely describe matter; it quietly diagnoses its quantum structure.

Complex heat capacity extends these possibilities further by giving experimental access to quantum memory and dynamical correlations. Many emerging quantum technologies rely not only on static entanglement, but on the controlled preservation of coherence[3] over time. Quantum sensors, quantum memories, and noisy intermediatescale quantum devices all struggle with the same problem: unwanted dissipation and decoherence. Because complex heat capacity directly probes how energy storage and dissipation compete across timescales, it provides a thermodynamic window into how “quantum” a system’s dynamics really are. A response that violates classical temporal bounds is not just philosophically interesting; it also signals the presence of genuinely quantum dynamical resources that we can exploit.

Then there are implications for quantum thermodynamic machines. Quantum heat engines, refrigerators, and batteries are often analysed using idealised models that assume specific forms of coherence or entanglement. Thermodynamic witnesses offer a way to verify, experimentally and in situ, whether or not those quantum resources are actually present during operation. Rather than inferring entanglement indirectly from performance metrics like efficiency or power, one could determine its presence or absence directly through calorimetric response. This tightens the feedback loop between theory and experiment and helps to distinguish genuinely quantum advantages from classical engineering.

At a more foundational level, these ideas influence how we think about the boundary between classical and quantum descriptions of Nature. Thermodynamics has long been framed as a theory of coarsegraining: a description of what happens when you stop caring about microscopic details. The discovery that thermodynamic quantities can witness entanglement, both in space and in time, forces a reassessment of that narrative. It suggests that quantum correlations are not automatically erased by scale, noise, or complexity. Instead, they can survive aggregation and manifest as robust macroscopic signatures. This insight feeds directly into ongoing debates about quantum-to-classical transitions, decoherence, and the emergence of irreversibility.

In this sense, thermodynamics is no longer merely a passive consistency check imposed on microscopic theories. It becomes an active interrogator of quantum structure, capable of revealing correlations that cannot be explained classically. What began as a theory of steam engines has quietly evolved into a diagnostic language for entanglement, memory, and dynamics—precisely the features that define the quantum world we are now trying to control.

More speculatively—but no less intriguingly—these ideas are beginning to resonate beyond traditional physics, particularly in biological and soft-matter systems, where energy flow, dissipation, and memory play a central role. Living systems are not quantum computers, nor are they delicately shielded from noise. But they _are_ exquisitely organised far from equilibrium, and they process energy in ways that often go beyond simple classical intuition. From this perspective, thermodynamics, rather than the wavefunctions of quantum mechanics, may be the most natural language for probing whether genuinely non-classical effects ever become relevant in biology.

Complex heat capacity already has been known to be relevant for biological matter because it probes slow, hierarchical dynamics. Proteins, membranes, and macromolecular complexes possess many internal degrees of freedom that relax on vastly different timescales. When such systems are driven by temperature changes, chemical gradients, or mechanical forcing, their response often exhibits pronounced memory effects. Measuring the frequency-dependent heat capacity of biological samples has long been used to study folding transitions, conformational rearrangements, and hydration dynamics. What the quantum thermodynamic perspective adds is a sharper interpretational framework: it tells us which kinds of memory can be fully classical, and which would exceed classical bounds if ever observed.

This matters because biological function often relies not just on structure, but on timing and coordination. Enzymatic activity, signal transduction, and energy transport in biomolecular networks depend on correlations across time—i.e., how past excitations influence future behaviour. In principle, complex heat capacity provides a way to quantify how information about energy fluctuations persists and propagates through such systems, without needing to track individual microscopic trajectories. Even if the correlations turn out to be entirely classical, thermodynamic bounds still offer a powerful diagnostic tool for distinguishing simple relaxation from genuinely long-lived, structured memory.

More provocatively, there is growing interest in whether certain biological processes exploit quantum coherence or entanglement in a functional, albeit transient, way. Examples often discussed include excitonic energy transport in photosynthetic complexes, avian magneto-reception, and olfactory sensing. These systems operate at ambient temperatures and in noisy environments—conditions usually considered hostile to quantum effects. Yet experiments increasingly suggest that some degree of quantum coherence can survive long enough to influence biological performance. Thermodynamic witnesses are attractive here precisely because they do not require microscopic control or isolation. If quantum correlations play any operational role, they must ultimately leave traces in how energy is absorbed, stored, and dissipated. Calorimetric and dynamical response measurements, therefore, offer a realistic route to testing quantum-biological hypotheses without relying on fragile, systemspecific probes.

There is also a conceptual payoff. Biology forces us to confront the thermodynamics of information processing in physical systems that are adaptive, self-organising, and perpetually out of equilibrium. Living organisms continuously measure, respond, and update their internal states based on external stimuli. From a physics standpoint, this raises deep questions about the relationship between memory, dissipation, and irreversibility. Temporal entanglement provides a sharp benchmark against which biological memory can be assessed. Even ruling out such correlations is informative: it delineates the boundary between classical biochemical computation and anything more exotic.

Crucially, none of this requires biology to be “quantum” in a sensational sense. The real lesson is more subtle. Thermodynamics offers a unifying framework in which quantum systems, classical matter, and living organisms can all be analysed using the same language of constraints, bounds, and responses. If biology ever skirts the edge of those bounds, thermodynamics will notice. And if it does not, thermodynamics will tell us why classical descriptions suffice.

In this light, the broader significance of thermodynamic witnesses becomes clear. They do not promise that quantum mechanics is secretly running life behind the scenes. What they promise instead is something more valuable: a principled, experimentally grounded way to ask where quantum mechanics _must_ end, where classical physics genuinely begins, and whether any interesting phenomena live in the narrow space between.

So yes, thermodynamics is a funny subject. But perhaps Sommerfeld’s real insight was not that confusion eventually fades, but that it becomes productive. Thermodynamics has a habit of looking finished while quietly refusing to be exhausted—the proverbial hydra of physics, if you will. From steam engines to quantum statistics to entanglement witnesses, its most fruitful moments have come precisely when its constraints felt too rigid, too universal, or slightly unsettling. If history is anything to go by, then treating thermodynamics as something to outgrow would be a mistake. If we take those constraints seriously, without trying to explain them away too quickly, they tend to guide us, almost inadvertently, toward deeper physics. Doing so is an invitation to keep asking better questions and making bolder conjectures, confident that thermodynamics will continue to answer them in its own, quietly provocative way.

[1] By _phenomenological_, physicists mean a theory formulated directly in terms of observable, macroscopic quantities and their empirical relationships, without specifying or assuming an underlying microscopic model. Classical thermodynamics is phenomenological in this sense, as its laws were inferred from experimental regularities in heat and work, rather than derived from atomic or statistical descriptions.

[2] Local hidden variables refer to hypothetical classical descriptions in which physical properties are assumed to have definite values prior to measurement (_hidden variables_), and influences cannot propagate faster than light (_local_). Such models can produce correlations, but only up to well-defined limits. Quantum mechanics predicts—and experiments confirm—correlations that exceed those limits.

[3] Quantum coherence refers to the preservation of definite phase relationships between different quantum states. The phase encodes the timing of the underlying quantum oscillations, and preserving it allows different states to interfere. If interactions with the environment randomise these phases—a process known as decoherence—the interference disappears, and the system’s behaviour becomes effectively classical.
